# Preface

It is completely impossible to practice and follow true virtues if we do not establish <term>divine ethics<note>original: "göttliche Sittenlehre." This refers to a moral system grounded in religious revelation and God’s laws, rather than one based purely on human logic or social custom.</note></term> as our foundation!

However brilliantly the <term>natural philosophers<note>original: "natürlichen Weltweisen." Literally "world-wise ones," this refers to secular thinkers or philosophers who rely on reason and the study of the natural world rather than divine scripture.</note></term> have depicted the practice of virtue and the shamefulness of <term>vice<note>original: "Laster." A term for immoral habits or character flaws.</note></term>, and have therefore exhorted us to observe the former and avoid the latter; one can indeed admire the concepts they held of virtue and vice, and the teachings left behind in their writings. Their instruction, however, can by no means be considered sufficient to provide the strength required for the practice of virtue and the avoidance of vice; rather, it is—

# Notes
## for unlearned readers. <note>original: "unstudirte Leser." This refers to laypeople or individuals who have not received a formal university education in theology or Latin.</note>

Anyone who wishes to examine our writings and learn to understand our meaning must first form a correct concept of the words found within them, as it would be difficult for those who have not studied to grasp our intent. We could indeed have exchanged these for others that are easier to understand, and made use of the words and expressions common in other theological writings, had we not found in the very composition <note>original: "Silbenfügung," literally "the joining of syllables." The author suggests that the specific structure or sound of these words carries a unique spiritual weight.</note> of the retained words something emphatic, evocative, stimulating to the powers of thought, encouraging, and reflective—which is the sole reason why we have kept them and made use of them.

**Magical:** <note>In the context of 18th-century mysticism, "magic" does not refer to sorcery, but to the internal, spiritual operations of divine grace or nature.</note> signifies, according to our meaning, mysterious powers incomprehensible to human understanding, whose effects can only be felt, but not seen.

**Moral:** modest, humble, lawful, as order requires.

--- Page 27 ---
<meta>continuity with previous page: This page continues the glossary intended for "unlearned readers" that began on the previous leaf. It transitions from defining "Magical" and "Moral" to explaining more complex mystical concepts such as the nature of spiritual light, darkness, and the formation of ideas within the soul.</meta>

**Moral Light:** an understanding enlightened by moral conduct, which organizes one's life and actions according to divine and worldly laws; in general: virtuous.

**Moral Darkness:** signifies, by contrast, when the understanding is darkened, the will corrupted, the actions evil, and in conflict with divine and human laws or established order; in general: vice-ridden.

**Divine Light-Power:** By this is actually to be understood that incomprehensibly active power emanating from the light of the wisdom of the Father and the Son, which is called "Spirit" in the Scriptures, or as it is also understood and accepted in other theological writings under the name of the Holy Spirit.

**Idea:** These are images which the human understanding and earthly reason form within the human spirit through the mediation and help of the soul-fire <note>original: "Seelenfeuers." In 18th-century mystical thought, this "fire" often represents the fundamental driving force or vital spark of the human soul.</note>, and which are either extinguished again in the power of thought <note>original: "Denkungskraft."</note> by the human will, or else visibly represented in essence, or committed through actions.

## On the Origin of Creation through the Will of God, or the Supreme Good.

God as God is in Himself the most perfect being, and requires no creature nor created thing <note>original: "Kreatur noch Geschöpfe." In this mystical context, the author uses both terms to emphasize the totality of everything brought into existence, from sentient beings to inanimate matter.</note> outside of Himself. His understanding consists in the purest and most glorious light. He is the self-existent light, which no one can approach. He has within Himself no ground <term>ground</term> (German: *Grund*). In the mystical tradition, this often refers to the *Ungrund*—the fathomless, bottomless nature of the Divine that precedes all definition or creation. His depth and height, His power and strength, are known and understood only by His own Spirit. No one can see Him; nevertheless, it is permitted for those spirits and humans endowed with understanding and will to search into His incomprehensible depths, in which, however, a ground can never be found, because He has no ground. ## On the Origin of Creation through the Will of God, or the Highest Good.

God, as God, is in Himself the most perfect Being, and requires no creature or creation outside of Himself. His understanding consists in the purest and most glorious light. He is the self-subsistent <note>original: "selbstständige." His depth and height, His power and strength, are known and recognized only by His own Spirit. To investigate this is entirely in vain, and is not permitted to us, because as finite creatures <term>Kreaturen</term> <note>In this context, "creatures" refers to any created being, including humans, as distinguished from the Creator.</note> we can find no foundation, but would rather lose our reason, fall into confusion, and commit the same error into which our first parents <term>Stammeltern</term> <note>A traditional term for Adam and Eve.</note> fell when they wished to be like God. 4. In this darkness, the active properties formed themselves into Nature <term>Natur</term>. Among these active properties, a conflict <term>Streit</term> <note>In the mystical tradition of Jacob Böhme, which this text follows, "Streit" refers to the dynamic tension or interaction between opposing forces that allows the physical world to manifest.</note> arose. Through this conflict, fire—as a moving and creative force in nature—became manifest, and light was born from the fire.

5. ## Chapter Four.

### On the possibility that morally good spirits can transform into morally evil spirits.

## Chapter Fifteen.
### Of the Light of Reason, and of the
### Light of Understanding.

Two **light-powers** were imparted to man at his creation, and are still imparted to all men at their birth. The one is the **light of reason**, and the second is the **light of conscience**.

2. We receive the **light of reason** from the **spirit of this world**, and we share this in common with all other animals. The **light of understanding** and **conscience**, however, is of a **heavenly quality**, and was imparted to the first man—and through him to all his descendants—from the **essence of God** itself; therefore, it may well [be] <note>The sentence concludes on the following page; the catchword provided is "kann" (can).</note> through reason

He who does not walk upon this correct path walks either in superstition or unbelief, and therefore cannot please God—even if he gave all his possessions to the poor and let his body be scorched and burned <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:3, emphasizing that outward sacrifice or martyrdom without inner transformation is spiritually worthless.</note>, and even if he confessed and took communion every day. ## Chapter Nineteen.

### On the Dual State of the Soul After Death and After Resurrection. And of what the Qualities of Heaven and Hell Consist.

In Himself, the Being called God is the highest and most perfect Light-spirit of wisdom and understanding. Outside of Himself, however, He has revealed Himself through two mighty powers—Light and Darkness—within nature and the created being. <note>This "Light and Darkness" dualism is a common theme in 18th-century mystical thought, suggesting that the physical and spiritual worlds are built upon opposing forces that find their origin in God's self-revelation.</note>

20. My dear reader, here you have the true image of a real **wise man**.
